Something is historic when it is so important and significant that it deserves to be remembered in history — or already is. The word does not simply mean "old" or "from the past." It means momentous, landmark, consequential — something that stands apart from ordinary events because of the impact it had or the change it caused.

A useful way to think about it: millions of things happen every single day. Most are forgotten within a week. A historic event is one that people will still be talking about years, decades, or even centuries later, because it changed something in a lasting, meaningful way.
The Single Most Important Distinction: "Historic" vs. "Historical"

This is arguably the most critical thing to understand about this word, because the two are very commonly confused — even by native speakers.

Historic = important and significant in history; worthy of being remembered.
Historical = simply relating to history or the past; anything that happened before now.

Read these pairs carefully:

  • "The signing of the peace treaty was a historic moment." (It was important and world-changing.)
  • "The professor studied many historical documents." (They are from the past — but may not be especially significant.)
  • "Neil Armstrong's moonwalk was a historic achievement." (Unprecedented; changed humanity forever.)
  • "The textbook covers historical events from the 18th century." (Simply events from the past — ordinary or not.)
  • "She visited a historic battlefield." (Famous because of what crucially happened there.)
  • "She is interested in historical research." (Research about the past in general.)

The golden rule: Every "historic" thing is also "historical" (it happened in the past), but not every "historical" thing is "historic" (not everything from the past is significant). "Historic" is a judgment of importance. "Historical" is simply a description of time.

Something earns the label "historic" when it meets one or more of these conditions:

  1. It is the first of its kind. The first woman elected as head of state. The first human in space. Firsts are almost always historic because they mark a before and an after.
  2. It marks a major turning point. A law that transforms society. A treaty that ends a war. A discovery that rewrites science. These shift the course of events permanently.
  3. It affects a very large number of people. The bigger the ripple, the more historic the event. A global pandemic, a world war, a landmark international agreement — all historic.
  4. It is unprecedented. Something never done before, or done at a scale never seen before, qualifies. Breaking a record that stood for a century, winning by a margin never achieved before.
  5. It will be remembered for a very long time. Short-term big news is not automatically historic. Something truly historic endures in collective memory.

Interestingly, you can call something "historic" before it actually happens, when you believe it will be remembered as significant. This is the anticipatory use of the word.

  • "Tomorrow's summit is expected to be a historic occasion."
  • "Scientists say this launch could mark a historic turning point in space exploration."

Here, the speaker is making a prediction — they believe the event will be so important that history will record it. This is perfectly correct usage.

"Historic" commonly appears with certain nouns. Knowing these collocations will help you use and recognize the word naturally:

  • Historic moment — a point in time of great significance
  • Historic victory — a win so notable it will be long remembered, often the first or the largest
  • Historic agreement / deal / treaty — a major pact that changes relations between parties
  • Historic occasion — a ceremonially or significantly important event
  • Historic achievement — an accomplishment of landmark importance
  • Historic landmark / site / building — a place famous for what happened there or what it represents
  • Historic decision — a choice with major, lasting consequences
  • Historic speech — a speech so powerful or important it is remembered long after it was delivered
  • Historic high / low — a level of something (a price, a temperature, a score) that surpasses all previous records
A Common Grammar Question: "A Historic" or "An Historic"?

In standard modern English, the correct form is "a historic" — not "an historic" — because the "h" in "historic" is pronounced, making it begin with a consonant sound. The same logic applies to "a hotel," "a hero," "a hypothesis." You say "a historic event," "a historic victory," "a historic agreement."

You may occasionally see "an historic" in older British texts, but this is now considered outdated. The modern standard on both sides of the Atlantic is "a historic."

When someone calls something "historic," they are making a strong statement: this matters, this will be remembered, this changed things. It is a word that elevates an event above the ordinary and places it in the permanent record of human experience.

Use "historic" for events, decisions, achievements, agreements, places, and occasions that are genuinely significant and lasting. Reserve "historical" for anything that simply has to do with the past, regardless of its importance. Get that distinction right, and you will use — and understand — both words with precision every time.
